content: The median age at diagnosis for cervical intraepithelial neoplasia grade III (CIN III) was 37 years (ranging from 15 to 83 years) among Italian-born women and 36 years (ranging from 19 to 68 years) among immigrant women. A study by Marlow in 2015 explored barriers to cervical cancer screening among women aged 28 to 63 years from white British and ethnic minority backgrounds in London. The qualitative interviews revealed significant knowledge deficits, particularly among older ethnic minority women, who highlighted a lack of awareness within their communities. The American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists recommended modifying the baseline age for cervical cancer screening to 21 years, regardless of the timing of first sexual intercourse. A study assessing abnormal cytologic diagnoses, particularly high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesions (HSIL), in a high-risk, low-income population of African American and Hispanic young adults found that delaying screening until age 21 was effective in detecting early precancerous lesions. Between 2001 and 2009, the overall abnormal cytology rate for women under 21 years was 25%, with HSIL accounting for 1%, atypical squamous cells (ASC-H/LSIL) for 3%, and low-grade squamous intraepithelial lesions (LSIL/ASC-US) for 22%. No cases of invasive squamous cell carcinoma were observed in this cohort before age 21. Persistent high-risk HPV infections were identified in 4% of women under 21, but none progressed to invasive carcinoma during the study. A U.S. population-based study by Simard in 2012 found that cervical cancer incidence rates among women under 50 years converged between Black and white women from 2005 to 2009, eliminating previous racial disparities. However, among women aged 50 to 64 years and those over 65, rates remained significantly higher for Black women throughout the study period. The authors suggested that differences in follow-up and treatment of precancerous lesions might explain these findings, despite similar screening rates between racial groups. A global review by Ting in 2010 highlighted that variations in the age pattern of HSIL across regions are likely due to differences in the initiation age, frequency, coverage, and follow-up rates of cervical cancer screening. Screening coverage varies significantly by country and region. In Brazil, a 2017 survey found that younger women (aged 25–35 years) had the poorest quality indicators for cervical cancer screening, including lack of access and guidance, compared to women aged 35–49 years and 50–64 years. The Jade Goody effect in the UK, following media coverage of her cervical cancer diagnosis and death, led to a significant increase in screening uptake and cancer diagnoses among women aged 27–29 years in 2009. In Ontario, a 2019 study identified gaps in cervical cancer screening correspondence programs, with women under 50 years being more likely to miss mailed invitations for screening. In Finland, the organized cervical cancer screening program invites women starting at age 25 or 30 (depending on the municipality) every five years. Despite low participation rates (51–61%) among women aged 25–35 years in the organized program, overall five-year Pap smear coverage, including opportunistic testing, is high (85–90%). Two-thirds of women aged 20–24 years, who are not yet eligible for organized screening, undergo testing outside the program. In the U.S. Without state and federal funding programs, this group remains underserved. In Australia, the National Cervical Screening Program has successfully reduced squamous cervical cancer incidence by at least 50% in women aged 25 years or older. However, its effectiveness among women under 25 has been limited. Since 2017, the program has introduced explicit invitations for screening, starting near a woman’s 25th birthday. A Swedish cohort study found that women unscreened or with abnormal results in their 50s had a higher risk of cervical cancer after age 60. Screening at ages 61–65 was associated with a significant risk reduction up to age 80. However, women with normal screening results in their 50s showed minimal additional benefit from screening after age 60. Studies on HPV prevalence and cervical cancer screening in women living with HIV (WLHIV) emphasize the importance of tailored screening strategies. The World Health Organization (WHO) is considering updates to its guidelines for cervical cancer prevention in WLHIV, focusing on age-specific screening and follow-up intervals. A systematic review identified gaps in evidence, particularly regarding the frequency of re-screening after successful treatment of precancerous lesions. However, available data suggest that WLHIV benefit from regular screening and follow-up to prevent cervical cancer progression.
